prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol or other centrally acting D2-blocking antiemetics or antipsychotics; if an antipsychotic is needed, use quetiapine or clozapine
Do not revise the diagnosis to PSP on the saccadic freezing alone: there is no vertical supranuclear gaze palsy or slowing of vertical saccades
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in this older patient
required_recommendations: Keep the diagnosis of PD: the saccadic freezing with a full vertical range, preserved optokinetic responses and a normal midbrain on MRI is not a supranuclear gaze palsy, and the oculomotor and motor worsening fit advancing PD on a low levodopa dose (300 mg/day after 8 years)
Increase levodopa (for example carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 one tablet four or five times daily, or 1.5 tablets three times daily) and reassess the eye movements and limb signs at follow-up
Arrange an orthoptic review of the convergence insufficiency (base-in prisms for near work) and continue ophthalmology follow-up of the left epiretinal membrane
Review clonazepam, which adds sedation and fall risk and can slow saccades: use the lowest effective dose or consider melatonin, tapering rather than stopping abruptly
Refer to physiotherapy for gait and balance because of the more frequent near-falls, and reassess the depression, which has worsened on sertraline 100 mg

alternatives: Melatonin for REM sleep behavior disorder has less sedation and fall risk than clonazepam.
interactions: Clonazepam adds sedation and fall risk with dopaminergic drugs in older patients, and benzodiazepines can lengthen saccade latency.
Sertraline with an MAO-B inhibitor: serotonin syndrome is rare; use the lowest dose and monitor. Fluoxetine and fluvoxamine are best avoided with rasagiline.
Amlodipine lowers standing blood pressure and levodopa can lower it further: measure lying and standing blood pressure as the levodopa dose rises.
general.summary: No dopamine-blocking drug on the list. Clonazepam: sedation, falls and slower saccades. Sertraline: caution with a future MAO-B inhibitor. Amlodipine with levodopa: additive hypotension.
warnings: Clonazepam: taper rather than stop abruptly if it is withdrawn.
Levodopa: nausea, postural hypotension and daytime sleepiness are possible at higher doses.

metadata.difficulty_description: Moderate difficulty due to prominent oculomotor abnormality (saccade freezing) that mimics atypical parkinsonian syndromes (PSP, CBD) and creates diagnostic uncertainty. The key insight is recognizing that these oculomotor symptoms are dopamine-responsive features of advancing PD rather than a separate diagnosis. Confounders include clonazepam use (which can affect saccades) and the left eye epiretinal membrane (contributing to visual symptoms).
metadata.difficulty_rationale: New saccadic freezing in long-standing PD suggests PSP; the agent must read the full vertical range and normal midbrain as PD on too low a levodopa dose, and see the near diplopia as convergence insufficiency. One required criterion (MRI).

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Dorothy Kowalski is a 68-year-old right-handed woman with an 8-year history of Parkinson's disease who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by her husband with a chief complaint of intermittent binocular diplopia and troubling episodes in which her eyes seem to 'freeze.' She reports that over the past three to four months, she has been experiencing intermittent double vision, particularly when reading or watching television. The diplopia resolves with monocular occlusion and is worse at near than at distance. More concerning to her is a new phenomenon that began approximately two months ago: during conversations or when trying to shift her gaze, she will suddenly find herself unable to move her eyes for what she estimates to be 15 to 20 seconds. During these episodes, she describes feeling 'locked in place' and becomes visibly distressed, stating that she tries to look but her eyes will not obey. Her husband confirms that he has witnessed these episodes multiple times and notes that her speech becomes more slurred and her blinking seems to stop during the freezing spells. He also observes that she sometimes can break out of the episodes by slowly tracking a moving object such as his hand, after which she can resume looking around but her eye movements seem 'slower and jerkier' for several minutes afterward. She denies any associated headaches, loss of consciousness, or limb weakness during these episodes. Her Parkinsonian motor symptoms have been gradually worsening over the past year despite stable dosing of carbidopa-levodopa 25-100 mg three times daily. She reports increased difficulty with fine motor tasks, worsening of her right-hand tremor, and more frequent near-falls. Her husband reports that her facial expression has become even more mask-like and her voice increasingly quiet. She also notes that her mood has worsened despite continued sertraline, and she has become more socially withdrawn. She takes clonazepam 0.5 mg at bedtime for REM sleep behavior disorder, diagnosed on a sleep study 5 years ago after her husband described her punching and shouting in her sleep; the episodes are now rare. She denies visual hallucinations, significant cognitive decline, or urinary incontinence. She was last seen by ophthalmology six months ago for monitoring of her left eye epiretinal membrane, which was stable. She has not had any recent changes in her medications.

neurological_exam.additional: Speech became noticeably slower and more dysarthric during the saccade testing episode, with further decrease in blink rate. Mild seborrheic dermatitis on forehead and nasolabial folds. No myoclonus. Glabellar reflex positive (fails to habituate).
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing intact without dysmetria bilaterally. Heel-to-shin testing intact. No cerebellar ataxia. Mild dysdiadochokinesia attributable to bradykinesia.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Visual acuity 20/25 OD, 20/40 OS with pinhole correction. Pupils equal round and reactive to light, 3mm bilaterally. No relative afferent pupillary defect. Visual fields full to confrontation. Optic disc margins sharp bilaterally. Extraocular movements full in all directions of gaze. No gaze-evoked nystagmus. Smooth pursuit slightly saccadic in horizontal and vertical planes. Convergence insufficiency noted at near. During reflexive saccade testing, patient demonstrated intermittent episodes of severe difficulty initiating saccades — approximately 20-second 'freezing' periods during which she was unable to generate voluntary horizontal or vertical saccades despite effortful attempts. No compensatory head thrust or blink to initiate saccades during these episodes. Patient was able to break freezing episodes by performing smooth pursuit, after which saccades resumed but were more hypometric with increased latency (approximately 7 seconds). Between episodes, horizontal reflexive saccades were mildly hypometric with latencies under 1 second. Optokinetic responses present and symmetric. Facial sensation intact bilaterally. Marked facial hypomimia with reduced blink rate. Hearing grossly intact. Palate elevates symmetrically. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.gait: Narrow-based shuffling gait with reduced stride length. Markedly reduced arm swing on the right, mildly reduced on the left. Mild festination on turns. Pull test: two retropulsive steps before correction. Able to rise from chair without using arms but slowly and with visible effort.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) score 27/30, losing points on trail-making (1) and delayed recall (2). Speech is hypophonic with mild dysarthria but fluent with intact comprehension and repetition. No aphasia, neglect, or apraxia. Affect mildly flat, consistent with both depression history and Parkinsonian hypomimia.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk mildly reduced in bilateral upper extremities. Right-hand resting tremor, 4-5 Hz, pill-rolling type, suppressed with voluntary movement. Moderate cogwheel rigidity at right wrist, mild at left wrist. Prominent bradykinesia on rapid alternating movements, worse on the right, with marked decrement in amplitude and speed during finger tapping. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffmann sign.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch and pinprick intact throughout. Proprioception intact at bilateral great toes. Vibration sense mildly diminished at bilateral ankles. Romberg negative.
